title: Borrowers’ cash flow squeeze gets ‘way too much attention’: RBA
full_text:
The Reserve Bank of Australia is trying to fight perceptions that interest rates solely work by punishing borrowers, and has shifted its messaging to stress how important the exchange rate is to monetary policy.
RBA modelling shows that fluctuations in the exchange rate in response to interest rate changes account for as much as two-thirds of the impact of monetary policy on GDP and inflation.
The bank’s recent emphasis on the exchange rate channel of monetary policy comes as it tries to rein in perceptions that the cash flow channel – the way rising interest rates restrict borrowers’ disposable incomes – is the main way monetary policy changes are flowing through the economy.
RBA assistant governor Chris Kent said on Monday the role of exchange rates in transmitting borrowing cost increases through to the rest of the economy “quickly gets forgotten”.
“All those [different channels of monetary policy] are working, and then the one that gets way too much attention – and we’ve said this before – is the cash flow channel,” Kent told the Commonwealth Bank’s Global Markets Conference on Monday.
When rates rise – as they have four times this year to take the cash rate to a 15-year high of 4.6 per cent – that improves the return on investment in Australia compared with the rest of the world.
Investors then buy more Australian dollars, which causes the currency to appreciate and makes imports cheaper and more attractive to domestic buyers. That eases demand for locally produced goods and saps heat from the domestic economy.
Kent’s comments echoed RBA governor Michele Bullock’s remark at her latest monetary press conference in September that exchange rates were “the most important channel” through which this year’s quadruple rate rise will flow through to the rest of the economy.
Westpac chief economist and former RBA official Luci Ellis said the more explicit references to exchange rates was a marked shift in communication from the bank earlier in the monetary policy tightening cycle.
“The real question is: why weren’t they talking about [the exchange rate channel] during the year?” Ellis said in an interview with The Australian Financial Review before Kent’s speech. She argued the central bank had made little of the Australian dollar’s rise above US72¢ earlier in the year when rates began rising.
“They haven’t been putting consistent weight on that channel, but it is there.”
HSBC chief economist for Australia and New Zealand Paul Bloxham said the RBA was trying to battle the perception that the cash flow channel was the major pipeline through which rate rises affected the economy.
“The reason the RBA is talking about the breadth of all the different channels is because they want to point out that actually this is just one of, and not necessarily even the largest, of the channels that affects the economy,” Bloxham said.
Rate rises a ‘painful experience’ for borrowers
The RBA has had to strike a delicate balance between communicating the impact of borrowing cost increases without being seen to trivialise their implications for individual borrowers.
That comes as commentators – such as media personality David Koch, who now works as economic director for Compare the Market – say households are being made to pay the price for excessive spending elsewhere in the economy, including from governments.
Kent noted that the public’s focus on the hit to borrowers’ cash flows as a result of recent rate rises made sense because it was the channel of monetary policy ordinary people best understood.
“It’s very tangible. I think it’s important for us to acknowledge that, because for mortgage holders that are struggling and haven’t had a chance to build up those buffers they can rely on, that really is a painful experience for them,” said Kent.
“It’s important to emphasise to people there are many channels, and the cash flow is probably the least important in terms of the macroeconomics.”
RBA research confirms the cash flow effect is small in aggregate terms, with a 1 percentage point increase in the cash rate amounting to an estimated 0.1 per cent to 0.2 per cent drop in aggregate household expenditure, and about a 0.2 per cent drop in total household disposable income.
However, the RBA’s staff have noted that the cash flow channel’s effect on individual households’ interest income and repayments was at “historical highs”, which may explain why borrowers viscerally feel its impact.
Economists say the channel’s importance has also been diminished by the large savings buffers built up by households – including in offset accounts linked to home loans – that have partly shielded mortgagors from rising interest rates.
“That can also somewhat blunt the impact through the cash flow channel,” said HSBC’s Bloxham. “It shows you that there’s all these other channels that work, and we focus too much on just this one particular, narrow way that monetary policy affects the economy.”
